clue.text: Personality has black-out arriving at this speed

indicators.note: something put out is removed, so one word's letter is taken away from the other

parts.note: a personality is a famous person, a celebrity
B is the pencil-grade abbreviation for black

explanation.surface: A famous figure suffers a blackout just as they arrive somewhere at speed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Black-out' reads as fainting, but it splits into black, the letter B, and out, its removal from CELEBRITY to leave CELERITY.
explanation.definitionFit: Celerity is a formal, somewhat literary word for swiftness of movement or action.

clue.text: It protects woods from intruders

parts.note: surface reading: something guarding a forest, like a gamekeeper
setter's reading: a preservative painted on timber to keep out insects and rot

explanation.surface: A guardian keeping trespassers out of the forest.
explanation.walkthrough: Woods suggests a forest; it means pieces of timber, such as fence panels.
explanation.definitionFit: Creosote is a tarry oil brushed onto fences and sheds to preserve timber against insects and fungal decay.

clue.text: Spear-carrying knave may be acting without pay

parts.note: a lance is a long spear
the jack is the knave in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: A rascal with a spear might be an unpaid actor.
explanation.walkthrough: A lance-jack is British army slang for a lance corporal, a rank once often held as an acting, unpaid appointment.
explanation.definitionFit: Lance corporals were historically soldiers given temporary, unpaid acting rank, so one may be acting without pay.

clue.text: Increase left out of the new serial

indicators.note: a new version is a remade one, so the remaining letters are rearranged
something left out of a group is omitted, so that letter goes missing

parts.note: L is the standard abbreviation for left
taken as written

explanation.surface: Something has been increased but omitted from the latest television serial.
explanation.definitionFit: To raise something is to lift it higher or make it greater, as in raising prices or wages.

clue.text: Terminal stop in this lodgement

parts.note: the toe is the terminal part of the foot
to hold is to stop or keep back

explanation.surface: A notice about the last stop on a line, at some lodging.
explanation.walkthrough: Terminal suggests a station; it is the far end of something, here the toe.
explanation.definitionFit: A toehold is a small foothold or initial position gained, a precarious lodgement from which to advance.

clue.text: Sounds like Pict country of old

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the word means picked, which is said exactly like Pict
second meaning: the former name of Korea under Japanese rule

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned remark that something resembles the ancient land of the Picts.
explanation.walkthrough: The Picts' old country suggests Scotland, but the second meaning is far away: Chosen was the name of Korea from 1910 to 1945.
explanation.definitionFit: Chosen equals picked, which is pronounced like Pict; separately, Chosen was the historical name used for Korea.

clue.text: Christmas rose that may restore balance

definitions.meaning: first meaning: the winter-flowering plant of that common name
second meaning: a herb prescribed in former times as a cure for madness

explanation.surface: A Christmas flower credited with power to steady someone.
explanation.walkthrough: Balance sounds physical, but here it is mental: the ancients prescribed this plant against insanity.
explanation.definitionFit: Hellebore is the genus of the Christmas rose, and black hellebore was a classical remedy for madness and melancholy.

clue.text: Having had more than enough of broken dates

indicators.note: a broken thing is in pieces, so the word's letters are put back together differently

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone sick of too many appointments that keep falling through, or of crushed dried fruit.
explanation.definitionFit: Sated means fully satisfied, with appetite filled to the point of wanting nothing further.

clue.text: Sharks making tenders

definitions.meaning: first meaning: nurse sharks, a kind of bottom-dwelling shark
second meaning: people who tend or look after the sick

explanation.surface: Swindlers putting in bids for a contract.
explanation.walkthrough: Sharks suggests swindlers and tenders suggests bids; both are meant literally, as fish and as carers.
explanation.definitionFit: Nurse sharks are a species of shark, and nurses are carers who tend patients in hospitals.

clue.text: Reams of paper — put it on the floor

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a long, tedious piece of writing
second meaning: a smooth layer of mortar spread over a concrete base

explanation.surface: An instruction to dump a stack of paper on the floor.
explanation.definitionFit: A screed is a lengthy written discourse, and also the levelled cement layer laid as a floor surface.

clue.text: Dissatisfaction at not having any interest

definitions.text: Dissatisfaction at not having any interest

parts.note: surface reading: someone unhappy, perhaps a saver earning nothing on their money
setter's reading: the weary discontent of finding nothing interesting at all

explanation.surface: A saver grumbles that their account pays no interest.
explanation.walkthrough: Interest suggests money in a bank; here it is the feeling of being engaged by something.
explanation.definitionFit: Ennui is listless boredom, a weary discontent arising from lack of anything to occupy or excite the mind.

clue.text: Short-haul flight carrier

parts.note: surface reading: a brief journey by aeroplane
setter's reading: a machine that carries people up a flight of stairs

explanation.surface: An airline operating brief hops between nearby airports.
explanation.walkthrough: Flight and carrier both point at airlines; the flight is of stairs.
explanation.definitionFit: A moving staircase transports passengers a short distance between floors, which is a flight of steps.

clue.text: Gustave follows the boy porter

parts.note: a boy's name, here standing for any boy
Gustave Doré was the French illustrator

explanation.surface: A man called Gustave walks behind a lad carrying luggage.
explanation.walkthrough: Gustave Doré, the nineteenth-century French illustrator, supplies his surname; 'follows' puts it after the boy.
explanation.definitionFit: A stevedore is a dock worker who loads and unloads cargo from ships, a porter at the docks.

clue.text: Supply bridge opponents with the fee

parts.note: East and North sit as opponents at the bridge table
a due is a fee or charge owed

explanation.surface: Paying a fee to the rival players at a bridge game.
explanation.walkthrough: In bridge, the four players are named by compass points, and East and North are on opposing sides.
explanation.definitionFit: To endue is to provide or endow someone with a quality or possession, so it means to supply.

clue.text: Caught the sort of bone that gets knocked

parts.note: a T-bone is a kind of steak bone, so the sort is T
rapped means knocked, as on a door

explanation.surface: Someone is caught out by the kind of bone that tends to get knocked, like a funny bone.
explanation.walkthrough: The sort of bone is the letter shape in T-bone steak.
explanation.definitionFit: Trapped means caught, held fast in a snare or confined with no way out.

clue.text: Out of control — having blown a fuse, perhaps

definitions.meaning: first meaning: unable to influence events
second meaning: without electricity after a fuse fails

explanation.surface: Someone loses their temper and runs wild.
explanation.walkthrough: Blowing a fuse sounds like an outburst of anger; here it is literal, an electrical circuit cut off.
explanation.definitionFit: Powerless means lacking authority to act, and also literally lacking an electrical supply after an outage.

clue.text: Old Penny Herries, windbag

parts.note: D stood for the pre-decimal British penny, from Latin denarius
Rogue Herries is Hugh Walpole's 1930 novel and its hero

explanation.surface: A list of names, Old Penny Herries, followed by a jibe at a talker.
explanation.walkthrough: Herries is the hero of Hugh Walpole's Lakeland novel Rogue Herries, so he is the rogue. Windbag sounds like an insult but is literal: a fabric bag that catches wind.
explanation.definitionFit: A drogue is a conical fabric sleeve, such as a windsock or sea anchor, that fills with air or water.

clue.text: Writers who do this get a type of stress

definitions.text: Writers who do this get a type of stress

parts.note: surface reading: authors who suffer from some job-related strain
setter's reading: drawing a line beneath words gives them emphasis

explanation.surface: Authors who work a certain way end up stressed.
explanation.walkthrough: Stress means emphasis, not anxiety.
explanation.definitionFit: To underline is to draw a line under words, the handwritten and typed way of marking emphasis.

clue.text: Last quarter of the autobahn round Europe needs re-making at this stage

indicators.note: going round something surrounds it, so one piece wraps the other
the final quarter of a word is its closing fourth, here two of its eight letters

parts.note: the final two of the eight letters of autobahn

indicators.note: remaking something builds it afresh, so the combined letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: The final section of a German motorway, ringing Europe, must now be rebuilt.
explanation.definitionFit: Hereupon is a formal adverb meaning immediately after this, at this point in proceedings.

clue.text: Joint holder is crooked to start with

parts.note: surface reading: a co-owner, or something holding a joint of a structure
setter's reading: the word's first four letters spell a synonym of crooked

explanation.surface: A shareholder in a joint venture is dishonest from the outset.
explanation.walkthrough: The joint is meat on a spit. SKEW, meaning crooked, starts the answer, but the last two letters are not clued.
explanation.definitionFit: A skewer is a long pin pushed through a joint of meat to hold it together while roasting.

clue.text: Highly exciting poker

definitions.meaning: second meaning: a fire poker heated until it glows

explanation.surface: A card game that is especially thrilling.
explanation.walkthrough: Poker reads as the card game; it is the fireside iron, famously red-hot.
explanation.definitionFit: Red-hot describes intense excitement and also a metal poker heated until it glows red.

clue.text: Put your foot down to get going

definitions.text: Put your foot down to get going

parts.note: surface reading: press the accelerator, or insist firmly
setter's reading: a foot pedal that drives a machine such as a sewing machine or loom

explanation.surface: A driver is urged to accelerate to get moving.
explanation.walkthrough: Putting your foot down usually means accelerating or being firm; here it is literal pressing of a pedal that powers a machine.
explanation.definitionFit: A treadle is a foot-operated lever that powers machines like old sewing machines, potter's wheels and spinning wheels.

clue.text: This takes the service to the consumer

definitions.text: This takes the service to the consumer

parts.note: surface reading: something delivering a business service to customers
setter's reading: the service is a set of cups and pot, carried to the drinker

explanation.surface: A business slogan about delivering service to customers.
explanation.walkthrough: Service sounds commercial, but it is a tea service, the set of cups, saucers and pot.
explanation.definitionFit: A tray is used to carry cups, saucers and teapot from the kitchen to those drinking.

clue.text: Sensational start for a spoilsport down under

parts.note: setter's reading: the answer begins with an exclamation meaning sensational
surface and definition: an Australian word for a killjoy

explanation.surface: A spoilsport in Australia gets off to a dazzling start.
explanation.walkthrough: Down under is Australia. WOW, meaning sensational, starts the answer; the remaining letters are not clued.
explanation.definitionFit: Wowser is Australian slang for a puritanical killjoy who disapproves of drinking and other pleasures.

clue.text: Wild cry follows him round the crag

parts.note: a round shape is a circle, the letter O
a scar is a steep rocky outcrop or cliff, a word common in northern English place names

explanation.surface: A climber's wild shout echoes after him as he works his way around a rocky crag.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a pun: 'Wild', cried out, sounds like Wilde, and the surname Wilde follows this first name. Scar for a crag is common in Yorkshire and the Lake District.
explanation.definitionFit: Oscar Wilde, the Irish playwright and wit, bore this first name, so his surname comes straight after it.

clue.text: Somerset town blacked, we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken rather than written, so the word is judged by sound

parts.note: charred means blackened by fire

explanation.surface: A town in Somerset has been blackened, so people say.
explanation.walkthrough: Chard is a market town in Somerset, a county in south-west England.
explanation.definitionFit: Chard is a town in south Somerset, England, best known as the birthplace of powered flight experiments.

clue.text: Sorcery to make Ariel bide

indicators.note: making something new from the given letters means rearranging them into another word

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A spell that would make Ariel, the sprite of The Tempest, stay put.
explanation.walkthrough: Ariel is Prospero's magical servant in Shakespeare's The Tempest, always eager to be freed, so sorcery forcing him to bide fits.
explanation.definitionFit: Diablerie is black magic or devilry, dealings with devils, so it is a word for sorcery.

clue.text: Rope in the "Dallas" solicitor

indicators.note: being in a phrase means sitting inside its run of letters, across the word break

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word and the start of the next

explanation.surface: A lawyer from the TV soap Dallas is roped into something.
explanation.walkthrough: Dallas was the American oil-family TV drama; 'Rope in' wants to be one phrase, but rope alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A lasso is a rope with a running noose used by cowboys for catching cattle, and to lasso is to rope.

clue.text: Assembly point for Johnnie

parts.note: surface reading: a place where people gather, as in a fire drill
setter's reading: Johnnie is an Edwardian admirer who waited for actresses after the show

explanation.surface: Directions telling a man named Johnnie where to gather.
explanation.walkthrough: Johnnie looks like a name, but stage-door johnnies were Edwardian admirers who hung about theatres hoping to meet chorus girls.
explanation.definitionFit: The backstage entrance of a theatre is where admirers waited for performers, so it was their gathering place.

clue.text: Be mean to winter sports representative

parts.note: skiing is the classic winter sport
a Member of Parliament represents a constituency

explanation.surface: Someone is told to be stingy towards a skiing official.
explanation.definitionFit: To skimp is to spend or provide too little, stinting on something, which is being mean or ungenerous.

clue.text: Shallow, like a forked — , said Falstaff

definitions.text: Shallow, like a forked — , said Falstaff

parts.note: surface reading: lacking depth; setter's reading: Justice Shallow in Henry IV Part 2
setter's reading: fill the gap with the vegetable in Falstaff's mocking description of the skinny Shallow

explanation.surface: A quotation-completion puzzle about a superficial person.
explanation.walkthrough: Shallow is not an adjective but Justice Shallow; in Henry IV Part 2 Falstaff remembers him as 'like a man made after supper of a cheese-paring', 'like a forked' root vegetable.
explanation.definitionFit: Falstaff compares the thin, spindly Shallow to a pale forked root vegetable with legs, completing his quotation.

clue.text: The French notary, curiously, is Austrian

indicators.note: doing something curiously means doing it in an odd way, so the letters come out in an odd order

parts.note: le is French for the
taken as written

explanation.surface: A French notary turns out, oddly, to be from Austria.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tyrol is an Alpine region of western Austria, so something Tyrolean is Austrian in origin.
